newsitem.title: FRANCE: French minister accuses UK of "social dumping".
newsitem.headline: French minister accuses UK of "social dumping".

text.p: European Affairs Minister Michel Barnier accused British firms on Monday of "social dumping" by sub-contracting staff to French companies to avoid paying France's higher social charges.

"I am horrified by the practices of British companies of which I have the proof," Barnier told reporters, choosing the same term British Prime Minister John Major used last week to condemn a French truck drivers' road blockade.
"This is not what Europe is about. We must put an end to these incitements to social dumping within the European Union," he said.

He produced a letter by a British firm, Hotel and Catering Staff Supplies Ltd of Rotherham, offering to recruit seasonal employees for hotels and restaurants in other European Union countries with the prospect of paying up to 30 percent less in payroll deductions.

Workers on six-month contracts would pay British national insurance contributions but would be entitled to full reciprocal coverage by the French public health service while employed in France, it said.
Barnier said the legal department of the French Foreign Ministry had examined the letter and advised him that such contracts would breach both French and EU law.
"It is a clear case of fraud. It is a circumvention of the French and European legislation," the minister said.

However, the director of the British firm, Charles Rhodes, told Reuters his system was entirely legal and was a cheaper way for French hotels to recruit British staff to serve their English-speaking clientele.
"There is no legal problem. The letter was approved by French lawyers with regard to the services supplied in France," he said.

Barnier appeared convinced that the scheme was also intended to recruit French nationals circumventing French social laws. The letter talks only about "European staff" without specifying their nationality.
"I suggest that Monsieur Barnier looks properly at what is written and he will perhaps see that it is not in contravention of French or European regulations," Rhodes said.
British firms have long taken advantage of EU legislation which allows staff on temporary contracts in other member states to continue paying their welfare contributions in their home country.

British service companies supply short-term labour to the construction industry in high-cost countries such as Germany and Britain, raising issues of respect for minimum wages, limits on working hours and other social regulations in those countries.

The French Communist party daily L'Humanite published another example on Monday, in which a British company based in Norwich wrote to a French construction firm offering staff who would work at least 50 hours a week without overtime, including Saturdays and Sundays.
